summary: Sets out IETF policy on the rights that contributors give when they submit material to the IETF, aiming to let authors keep as many rights as possible while allowing the work to be published and used. It is a Best Current Practice that obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 and updates RFC 2026.

eli5.summary: When you give a drawing to a club, you have to say what the club may do with it. This memo spells out what people give the IETF when they hand in their ideas.

questions: what rights do ietf contributors grant
who owns the copyright in an rfc
subtitle: What you hand over to the IETF Trust when you submit an idea, and what you get to keep.

tldr.problem: To publish and work on people's submissions, the IETF needs legal permission to copy, translate and adapt them, but authors want to keep as many of their own rights as possible.
tldr.mechanism: Anyone who submits a Contribution is deemed to agree to grant the IETF Trust a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide, sublicensable license, and to make a few representations about their right to do so.
tldr.outcome: Authors keep ownership of their Contributions, while the IETF Trust owns the copyright in the published RFC as a collective work. The memo obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 and covers copyright and similar rights, not patents.

today: RFC 5378 is a Best Current Practice (BCP 78) published in November 2008, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It obsoleted RFC 3978 and RFC 4748; the companion patent policy is now RFC 8179.

sections.title: Purpose and Scope of the Policy
sections.content:
RFC 5378 (BCP 78) is the IETF policy on rights in Contributions. Under the laws of most countries, authors get copyrights and other rights in their work automatically, and if the work is done in the course of employment, those rights often belong to the employer. For a Contribution to be used in the IETF Standards Process, including publication as an Internet-Draft or RFC, certain limited rights must be granted to the IETF Trust, which then grants the necessary rights to the IETF.

The memo is limited to copyright-style rights. Patent rights are handled by BCP 79 (RFC 3979), and the memo says it is not intended to address those issues. It obsoletes RFC 3978 and RFC 4748 and, with BCP 79 and RFC 5377, replaces Section 10 of RFC 2026. It is not legal advice.

Sections 1, 2, 5 and 6 are normative; the others are informative. The memo has no retroactive effect: it does not obtain additional rights from Contributions that predate the date the IETF Trust announces adoption of these procedures.
sections.eli5: Before the club can put your drawing in its newsletter, you have to say that is okay. This memo is the club rule for that, and it does not reach back to drawings handed in before the rule began.

sections.title: Key Definitions
sections.content:
A Contribution is any submission intended for publication as all or part of an Internet-Draft or RFC, plus any statement made within the context of an IETF activity. That includes oral statements in IETF sessions and written or electronic communications to plenary sessions, working groups, BOFs, the IESG, the IAB, IETF mailing lists, the RFC Editor or the Internet-Drafts function. Statements clearly not meant as input to an IETF activity are not Contributions.

A Contributor is the individual submitting it. An Indirect Contributor is anyone who materially or substantially contributed without being personally involved in the submission. The IETF Trust is a trust established under the laws of the Commonwealth of Virginia, USA, to hold and administer intellectual property rights for the benefit of the IETF.

The Legend Instructions are the standardized text maintained by the IETF Trust, with the rules for including it in IETF Documents. Reasonably and personally known means something a person knows personally or, because of their job, would reasonably be expected to know, so an organization cannot keep a person in the dark to avoid an obligation.
sections.eli5: A Contribution is anything you hand in or say out loud to the club for its projects. The Trust is the club's treasurer for ideas, keeping safe the permissions everyone gives.

sections.title: Why the Rules Look This Way
sections.content:
The main goal is to obtain from authors only the non-exclusive rights needed to develop and publish IETF Documents. Authors keep all other rights but cannot withdraw the rights they have granted. The IETF Trust holds the rights and sublicenses them to all IETF participants for use in the IETF Standards Process, and may grant other sublicenses guided by RFC 5377.

The IETF asks for assurances that Contributors have the authority to grant these rights, because copyright comes into existence when a work is created and the IETF cannot use a Contribution without sufficient rights. The assurances are requested only to the extent of the Contributor's reasonable and personal knowledge.

The right to produce derivative works lets the IETF evolve documents as deployment experience accumulates. The right to produce translations is required before any Contribution can be published as an RFC. Derivative works beyond translations are required for all Standards Track documents and for most others, with two exceptions: documents describing proprietary technologies and republications of other standards organizations' work. In those cases a special legend tells readers about the restriction.

Contributions not subject to copyright, such as those produced by the U.S. government or in the public domain, are still asked to carry the same grants and representations, to the extent the Contribution may be protected.
sections.eli5: The club only asks for the permissions it really needs, like copying your drawing and translating its caption. You keep everything else, and you cannot take back what you already allowed.

sections.title: Agreement by Submission and Confidentiality
sections.content:
By submitting a Contribution, each person actually submitting it and each named co-Contributor is deemed to have read and understood these rules and to have entered into a legally-binding agreement to comply with them. No further acknowledgment, signature or other action is required.

The Contributor is also deemed to have obtained the necessary permissions from any party the Contributor reasonably and personally knows may have rights in the Contribution, including a sponsor or employer.

No information subject to a confidentiality requirement or restriction on dissemination may be submitted as a Contribution or otherwise considered in the IETF Standards Process. A statement in a Contribution, even an automatically generated one, that claims confidentiality or privilege can be disregarded and has no force or effect.
sections.eli5: Handing something in counts as saying yes to the rules, with no form to sign. And you cannot hand in a secret, because anything given to the club is meant to be shared.

sections.title: The License Granted to the IETF Trust
sections.content:
To the extent a Contribution is protected by copyright or other rights of authorship, the Contributor and each named co-Contributor grant the IETF Trust a perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide, sublicensable license. It lets the Trust copy, publish, display and distribute the Contribution, prepare translations, prepare derivative works unless the notices in the Contribution explicitly disallow them, and reproduce trademarks in it solely in connection with reproducing and publishing the Contribution.

The Trust sublicenses these rights to all IETF participants for use within the IETF Standards Process under a license agreement it issues, and may grant further sublicenses in line with RFC 5377.

The grant is not a patent license: it does not give any right under a patent or patent application disclosed under BCP 79 or otherwise. Contributors claiming trademark rights in terms used in a Contribution are requested to state what conditions apply to implementers.
sections.eli5: You let the club's treasurer copy and share your drawing, forever and for free, and the treasurer can pass that permission to club members. Letting them copy the drawing does not let them use your invention.

sections.title: Representations, RFC Copyright and Retained Rights
sections.content:
Each Contributor represents, to the best of their knowledge and ability, that the Contribution properly acknowledges all Contributors including Indirect Contributors, that nothing in it is confidential, that nothing limits their ability to make these grants, that they have not intentionally included defamatory, untrue or illegal material, and that trademarks and proprietary names are clearly designated as such where reasonable.

The IETF has no duty to publish any Contribution and may withdraw or stop using one that does not comply.

Contributors or their sponsors keep ownership of their underlying Contributions. But for an RFC, other than an RFC Editor Contribution, each Contributor acknowledges that the copyright in the RFC as a collective work is owned by the IETF Trust, and is deemed to assign that interest on submission. The IETF Trust is directed to issue a license or assurance confirming that Contributors may use their Contributions as published in an RFC in any way they wish, with one restriction: nobody may represent a document as an RFC, or the equivalent, unless it is a full and complete copy or translation of the published RFC.
sections.eli5: You promise the drawing is really yours to share and not a copy of someone else's. The club owns the finished newsletter, but you can still use your own drawing however you like.

sections.title: Legends, Notices and Other Non-IETF Documents
sections.content:
Certain standardized text, such as copyright notices and disclaimers, must be reproduced verbatim in IETF Documents, including copies, derivative works and translations. The text and the rules for using it live in the Legend Instructions maintained by the IETF Trust, and the version that applies is the one posted on the publication date. The IETF may refuse to publish Contributions that lack the required legends. The legends themselves convey no rights; the grants come from this policy. Additional copyright notices are not permitted except for joint development with, or republication of, another standards organization, and only with approval by the IAB.

The memo applies to Contributions made in the IETF process. Documents submitted to the RFC Editor independently are called non-IETF documents and are not covered unless the controlling entity for that document stream applies these rules. Section 11 records an IAB declaration that the IAB stream is covered, and that other streams need their own discussion and approval process.

The Security Considerations section says there are no known security issues with Contribution rights policies.
sections.eli5: Some official stickers must be copied exactly onto every copy of the newsletter. The stickers only tell people the rules and do not give any permission by themselves.

sections.title: What Changed Since RFC 3978
sections.content:
The memo is a significant reorganization and rewording of RFC 3978. The most basic change limits it to the rights a Contributor grants to the IETF Trust; all sublicenses for using IETF Documents must come from the Trust. Material from RFC 4748 recognizing the IETF Trust was added.

Most material on RFC Editor documents was removed, and those documents were renamed non-IETF documents. New definitions were added for Contribution, Indirect Contributor, Copyright, IETF Trust and Legend Instructions. Responsibility for the text of notices moved to the IETF Trust.

The memo also makes clear that submitting a Contribution creates a legally binding contract, that it does not deal with patent licenses, who owns the copyright in IETF Documents, and what rights authors retain. The derivative-works right is no longer limited to use within the IETF Standards Process.
sections.eli5: The club rewrote its old rulebook so that one treasurer hands out the permissions and the rules are easier to follow.

messages.label: License grant
messages.note: Perpetual, irrevocable, non-exclusive, royalty-free, world-wide, sublicensable.

messages.label: Sublicense
messages.note: For use within the IETF Standards Process.

items.title: Copy and publish
items.text: Copy, publish, display and distribute the Contribution, in whole or in part.

items.title: Translate
items.text: Prepare translations into languages other than English.

items.title: Derivative works
items.text: Modify or build on it, unless the notices in the Contribution disallow it.

items.title: Trademarks
items.text: Reproduce trademarks in it, solely in connection with publishing the Contribution.
